claim: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
source_text: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
evidence_reasoning: This is a general statement reflecting established scientific understanding about microbial community function.

claim: Understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
source_text: However, understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects a known challenge in the field and is inferred from the complexity of natural systems.

claim: In strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other.
source_text: We found that in strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding supported by simulations and experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Partner intermixing in strong cooperation is insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
source_text: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing intermixing under various initial conditions.

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges.
source_text: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
source_text: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges and a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations of D. vulgaris and M. maripaludis biofilms.

claim: In simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
source_text: Even in simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from multi-species communities.

claim: When ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
source_text: Thus, when ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and simulation data presented.

claim: In a synthetic community, three bacterial species, each contributing an essential benefit while simultaneously competing for these benefits, can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance.
source_text: Consider microbial communities: in a synthetic community, three bacterial species, each contributing an essential benefit while simultaneously competing for these benefits, can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance (Kim et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a reference to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth.
source_text: different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth (Christensen et al., 2002; Brenner and Arnold, 2011)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by references to Christensen et al., 2002 and Brenner and Arnold, 2011.

claim: Branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface.
source_text: branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface (Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a reference to Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004.

claim: In waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates.
source_text: and in waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates (Satoh et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a reference to Satoh et al., 2007.

claim: It is still unclear how cell–cell and cell–environment interactions govern the patterning of communities.
source_text: it is still unclear how cell–cell and cell–environment interactions govern the patterning of communities (Elias and Banin, 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This reflects a gap in scientific knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: It is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community.
source_text: Thus, it is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community (Christensen et al., 2002; Wilmes et al., 2008; Dekas et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple references documenting pattern variability.

claim: Strong cooperation is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling to pathogenic biofilms.
source_text: This is because 1) it is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling (Schink, 2002; Falkowski et al., 2008; McInerney et al., 2009) to pathogenic biofilms (Kelly, 1980; Kolenbrander et al., 2010; Elias and Banin, 2012)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations and reflects established knowledge.

claim: The codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells.
source_text: and 2) the codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells (Schink, 2002; McInerney et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations and reflects a known challenge in microbiology.

claim: Cells initially divided and pushed other cells to the side such that all cells remained in the same plane.
source_text: Starting from one budding cell (a, hour 0.5), cells initially divided and pushed other cells to the side such that all cells remained in the same plane (b, hour 9).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on direct observation of yeast cell growth in Video 1.

claim: When the group of cells reached approximately 5-cell radius, cells in the center could no longer push other cells to the side and instead budded upward.
source_text: When the group of cells reached approximately 5-cell radius (c, hour 14), cells in the center could no longer push other cells to the side and instead budded upward, as indicated by higher intensities in the fluorescence images.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on direct observation of yeast cell growth patterns.

claim: The fitness model predicts that strong interactions beneficial to at least one partner can potentially lead to the convergence of initially disparate population ratios.
source_text: The fitness model predicts that strong interactions beneficial to at least one partner can potentially lead to the convergence of initially disparate population ratios (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction from the fitness model supported by simulation data.

claim: Vertical cross-sections of single-cell thickness from cooperative communities show significantly more intermixing than those from other communities.
source_text: Vertical cross-sections of single-cell thickness from cooperative communities show significantly more intermixing than those from other communities (n = 28 sections; p<0.01, Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: An intermixing index of 6 or above separates cooperative from non-cooperative communities in simulations.
source_text: An intermixing index of 6 (red dotted line) or above separates cooperative from non-cooperative communities in our simulations.
evidence_reasoning: This is a threshold determined from simulation results.

claim: For interactions benefiting at least one partner, including cooperation, commensalism, and exploitation, different initial partner ratios can potentially converge over time.
source_text: Simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1) and analytical calculations ('Requirements for steady-state ratios in the six types of communities' in 'Materials and methods') show that for interactions benefiting at least one partner, including cooperation ([↑ ↑]), commensalism ([∼ ↑]), and exploitation ([↓ ↑]), different initial partner ratios can potentially converge over time (Figure 1B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by both simulation data and analytical calculations.

claim: Population ratios converged in the commensal and cooperative but not competitive yeast communities.
source_text: Using engineered competitive, obligatory commensal, and obligatory cooperative yeast communities (see below), we confirmed that population ratios converged in the commensal and cooperative but not competitive communities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental data from engineered yeast communities.

claim: Convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply.
source_text: This convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply (Shou et al., 2007)
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation supported by a citation and logical inference.

claim: In competition, commensalism, and mutual antagonism, red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other.
source_text: In [∼ ∼], [∼ ↓], and [↓ ↓], red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other (Figure 1C–E).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results shown in the figures.

claim: In exploitation and commensalism, frequently one of the populations either formed a column or became covered by the partner population.
source_text: In [↑ ↓] and [∼ ↑], frequently one of the populations (green) either formed a column or became covered by the partner population (red) (Figure 1F–G).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results shown in the figures.

claim: Only in cooperation conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively intermixed.
source_text: Only in cooperation ([↑ ↑]) conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively 'intermixed', manifested as the two different cell types successively piling on top of each other (Figure 1H).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results shown in the figure.

claim: Statistically significant differences in intermixing were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions.
source_text: Statistically significant differences were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions (Figure 1I).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: Partner intermixing distinguishes strong cooperation from other ecological interactions.
source_text: Thus, we predicted that partner intermixing would distinguish strong cooperation from other ecological interactions.
evidence_reasoning: This is a prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: In obligatory commensal communities, since one supplier could support the birth of multiple consumers, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers.
source_text: In obligatory commensal communities, since one supplier could support the birth of multiple consumers, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers (top-views in B and vertical cross-sections in E).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations and logical inference about the stoichiometry of supply and consumption.

claim: Obligatory cooperative communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views and patchy cross-section patterns.
source_text: Obligatory cooperative communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views (C, 6× magnification insets in experiments) and patchy cross-section patterns (F).
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations.

claim: The intermixing index increased linearly with community height in obligatory cooperative communities.
source_text: In contrast, the intermixing index in obligatory cooperative communities increased proportionally to community height in both experiments and the diffusion model (Figure 2G, magenta).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by quantitative analysis of both experimental and simulation data.

claim: The proportionality of intermixing index to community height suggested the existence of a characteristic patch size of 10–20 µm.
source_text: This proportionality suggested the existence of a characteristic patch size ('Spatial analysis' in 'Materials and methods'), denoted λz*, of 10–20 µm.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the linear relationship observed in the data.

claim: The characteristic patch size was independent of initial conditions.
source_text: The characteristic patch size was independent of initial conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data under various initial conditions.

claim: If cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished.
source_text: Using the diffusion model, we found that if cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the diffusion model.

claim: Local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to take turns to grow, which leads to population intermixing.
source_text: Based on this result and based on patterns observed in top-views and vertical cross-sections of cooperative communities, we propose that local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to 'take turns' to grow, which leads to population intermixing (Figure 2H).
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed based on observed patterns and simulation results.

claim: In communities engaging in strong cooperation, but not in communities governed by other types of ecological interactions, the intermixing index increases proportionally as a function of community height.
source_text: In summary, in communities engaging in strong cooperation, but not in communities governed by other types of ecological interactions, the intermixing index increases proportionally as a function of community height.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the experimental and simulation findings.

claim: The proportionality of intermixing index to community height is due to a fixed patch size determined by localized nutrient supply and consumption.
source_text: This proportionality is due to a fixed patch size determined by localized nutrient supply and consumption.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the data.

claim: Intermixing was insensitive to initial conditions in the yeast obligatory cooperative communities.
source_text: We found that intermixing was insensitive to initial conditions in the yeast obligatory cooperative communities.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data under various initial conditions.

claim: The initial partner ratio did not significantly affect the level of intermixing.
source_text: The initial partner ratio did not significantly affect the level of intermixing
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Obligatory cooperative communities showed high population intermixing at the edges even when initiated from high-density inoculation spots.
source_text: edge sections ('Edge') of obligatory cooperative communities showed significantly more intermixing than those from non-cooperative communities (Mann–Whitney U test, p<5 × 10−5).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits required greater community heights to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
source_text: In simulations using the fitness model, facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits required greater community heights to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model.

claim: Partner intermixing is insensitive to diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm2/s.
source_text: In the diffusion model, obligatory cooperative communities with diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm2/s (corresponding to the diffusion constants of Sulforhodamine 101 in yeast community and agarose, respectively) both showed significant partner intermixing during growth.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the diffusion model.

claim: Partner intermixing is insensitive to the kinetics of interactions.
source_text: Partner intermixing is insensitive to the kinetics of interactions. With or without incorporating details such as significantly better starvation tolerance in adenine-requiring cells compared to lysine-requiring cells and the consequent delay in lysine release compared to adenine release (Shou et al., 2007), the diffusion model (lines) yielded substantial population intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the diffusion model.

claim: Intermixing does not depend on asymmetry between cooperating partners.
source_text: Intermixing does not depend on asymmetry between cooperating partners. We examined symmetric obligatory cooperation by assuming that for the two partners, all live cells released nutrients at a constant and identical rate without delay, and that other properties such as rates of growth, death, and nutrient consumption were also identical. Partner intermixing in this symmetric obligatory cooperative system (Sym. coop) was similar to that in asymmetric obligatory yeast cooperative system (Coop).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results comparing symmetric and asymmetric cooperation.

claim: Cooperative intermixing is insensitive to initial ratios.
source_text: Cooperative intermixing is insensitive to initial ratios.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data from engineered yeast communities.

claim: Intermixing relies on spatial localization of cooperative benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners, and is otherwise insensitive to initial conditions or the detailed kinetics of interactions.
source_text: Together, these results suggest that intermixing relies on spatial localization of cooperative benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners, and is otherwise insensitive to initial conditions or the detailed kinetics of interactions.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental and simulation results.

claim: Desulfovibrio vulgaris ferments lactate and produces mainly acetate, CO2, and H2.
source_text: Dv ferments lactate and produces mainly acetate, CO2, and H2.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the metabolism of D. vulgaris.

claim: The fermentation reaction of D. vulgaris is not thermodynamically favorable unless H2 is kept at very low concentrations.
source_text: However, this reaction is not thermodynamically favorable unless H2 is kept at very low concentrations.
evidence_reasoning: This is established thermodynamic knowledge about the fermentation reaction.

claim: H2 produced by D. vulgaris is used by M. maripaludis to reduce CO2 to methane.
source_text: H2 is used by Mm to reduce CO2 to methane.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the metabolism of M. maripaludis.

claim: In cooperative biofilms of D. vulgaris and M. maripaludis, the intermixing index increased with height.
source_text: In cooperative biofilms of Dv (green) and Mm (red), the intermixing index increased with height.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations of the biofilms.

claim: Vertical cross-sections of independent D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilms exhibited increasing intermixing as a function of community height.
source_text: Vertical cross-sections of independent D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilms indeed exhibited increasing intermixing as a function of community height (Figure 4B).
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations.

claim: Naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
source_text: Thus, naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilm data.

claim: Other known cooperative communities, including those degrading herbicide pollutants and those colonizing teeth, also seemed to display intermixed patterns.
source_text: Other known cooperative communities, including those degrading herbicide pollutants (Breugelmans et al., 2008) and those colonizing teeth (Palmer et al., 2001) also seemed to display intermixed patterns
evidence_reasoning: This is based on observations from cited literature.

claim: In communities with more than two species, indirect interactions can obscure direct interactions.
source_text: In communities with more than two species, indirect interactions can obscure direct interactions
evidence_reasoning: This is a general principle in ecology applied to the multi-species context.

claim: Most of the cooperative pairs intermixed in simulated multi-species communities.
source_text: Quantifying intermixing in a total of 240 interactions from 24 independent communities showed that most of the cooperative pairs intermixed (magenta).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claim: Indirect interactions through other community members could make cooperative pairs not intermixed or non-cooperative pairs intermixed.
source_text: Indirect interactions through other community members could make cooperative pairs not intermixed (grey) or non-cooperative (commensal) pairs intermixed (brown).
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the simulation results of multi-species communities.

claim: Interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner can potentially result in ratio convergence.
source_text: The first expectation is that interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner ([↑ ↑], [∼ ↑], and [↓ ↑]) can potentially result in ratio convergence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is a general conclusion drawn from simulation and experimental data.

claim: Ratio convergence confers stability to community composition.
source_text: Ratio convergence confers stability to community composition.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the consequences of ratio convergence.

claim: In cooperation and commensalism, global stability can be achieved whereas in exploitation, local stability can be achieved.
source_text: An analytical calculation based on the fitness model showed that in [↑ ↑] and [∼ ↑], global stability can be achieved whereas in [↓ ↑], local stability can be achieved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; 'Requirements for steady-state ratios in the six types of communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence_reasoning: This is based on analytical calculations from the fitness model.

claim: In competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value.
source_text: In contrast, in competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value which will remain unchanged until the next perturbation.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference from the fitness model about equal-fitness competition.

claim: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
source_text: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference from the fitness model about unequal-fitness competition.

claim: In amensalism and mutual antagonism, population ratios at best have an unstable fixed point.
source_text: In amensalism and mutual antagonism, population ratios at best have an unstable fixed point (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on analytical calculations from the fitness model.

claim: Competing bacterial species form a columnar or layered pattern.
source_text: For instance, competing bacterial species form a columnar or layered pattern (Palmer et al., 2001; Kreth et al., 2005; An et al., 2006; Hallatschek et al., 2007; Bernstein et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Burkholderia sp. LB400 and Pseudomonas sp. B13(FR1) show spatial segregation as competitors when grown on citrate.
source_text: Burkholderia sp. LB400 and Pseudomonas sp. B13(FR1) show spatial segregation as competitors when grown on citrate
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2000.

claim: When Burkholderia sp. LB400 and Pseudomonas sp. B13(FR1) are grown on chlorobiphenyl they engage in metabolic commensalism and exhibit a layered pattern.
source_text: but when grown on chlorobiphenyl they engage in metabolic commensalism and exhibit a layered pattern (Nielsen et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2000.

claim: When grown on a non-selective carbon source, Comamonas testosteroni WDL7 outcompeted and covered Variovorax sp. WDL1.
source_text: Similarly, when grown on a non-selective carbon source, Comamonas testosteroni WDL7 outcompeted and covered Variovorax sp. WDL1
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Breugelmans et al., 2008.

claim: When C. testosteroni WDL7 and Variovorax sp. WDL1 are fed with an aromatic compound as the sole carbon source, competition switched to cooperation and the two populations intermixed.
source_text: but when fed with an aromatic compound as the sole carbon source, competition switched to cooperation and the two populations intermixed (Breugelmans et al., 2008).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Breugelmans et al., 2008.

claim: Cooperative oral bacteria species intermixed when grown on saliva.
source_text: Cooperative oral bacteria species intermixed when grown on saliva (Palmer et al., 2001; Periasamy and Kolenbrander, 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 2001 and Periasamy and Kolenbrander, 2009.

claim: Examining whether the intermixing index increases linearly as a function of community height will be informative to exclude transient increases.
source_text: If cooperative intermixing is suspected, then examining whether the intermixing index increases linearly as a function of community height will be informative to exclude transient increases.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological recommendation based on the findings.

claim: Different types of molecular mechanisms can conceivably alter patterning.
source_text: Fitness effects of ecological interactions rely on molecular mechanisms to manifest themselves. Different types of molecular mechanisms can conceivably alter patterning.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms that could affect patterning.

claim: If at least one population actively moves or grows hyphae to penetrate the entire community, two populations might appear intermixed even if they do not cooperate.
source_text: However, it is conceivable that if at least one population actively moves (Houry et al., 2012) or grows hyphae to penetrate the entire community, two populations might appear intermixed even if they do not cooperate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential alternative mechanisms for intermixing.

claim: In biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two populations differing only in fluorescent colors showed modest intermixing even though the expectation for equal-fitness competition is a columnar pattern.
source_text: In biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two populations differing only in fluorescent colors (Klausen et al., 2003) showed modest intermixing even though the expectation for equal-fitness competition is a columnar pattern with an intermixing index close to zero (Figure 2D, left).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Klausen et al., 2003.

claim: The modest intermixing in P. aeruginosa biofilms was caused by P. aeruginosa differentiating into non-motile stalk cells that anchored to the surface and motile cells that climbed up to form the mushroom-like caps.
source_text: This modest intermixing was caused by P. aeruginosa differentiating into non-motile 'stalk' cells that anchored to the surface and motile cells that climbed up to form the mushroom-like caps (Klausen et al., 2003).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Klausen et al., 2003.

claim: Environmental influences can also alter ecological patterning.
source_text: Environmental influences can also alter ecological patterning.
evidence_reasoning: This is a general principle about environmental effects on patterning.

claim: If two cooperating populations have very different preferences for oxygen, then the two populations are likely not to intermix and instead form layers.
source_text: For instance, if two cooperating populations have very different preferences for oxygen, then the two populations are likely not to intermix and instead form layers in which the aerobic population is exposed to oxygen while the anaerobic population is protected from oxygen.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative example of how environmental factors could affect patterning.

claim: Variability in patterning has been observed within and between communities.
source_text: Variability in patterning has been observed within and between communities (Christensen et al., 2002; Wilmes et al., 2008; Dekas et al., 2009)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations documenting pattern variability.

claim: Stochastic events such as environmental variability, mutations, or fluctuations in initial conditions can all lead to variable patterns.
source_text: Stochastic events such as environmental variability, mutations, or fluctuations in initial conditions can all lead to variable patterns.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about sources of pattern variability.

claim: If the straight-columnar pattern expected for equal-fitness competition is observed for the majority of community but a layered pattern is observed in occasional locations, then fitter mutants may have arisen in these locations.
source_text: For instance, if the straight-columnar pattern expected for equal-fitness competition is observed for the majority of community but a layered pattern is observed in occasional locations, then fitter mutants may have arisen in these locations, initiating unequal-fitness competition (Hallatschek et al., 2007; Korolev et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference supported by citations about mutant emergence.

claim: For mutually antagonistic interactions, the fitness model showed that population ratios can quickly diverge.
source_text: For mutually antagonistic interactions, the fitness model showed that population ratios can quickly diverge.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model.

claim: In mutually antagonistic interactions, which population eventually dominates depends on the initial population ratio.
source_text: Thus, which population eventually dominates depends on the initial population ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: In mutually antagonistic interactions, stochastic variations in initial conditions can result in dramatically different patterns, giving rise to a phenomenon equivalent to survival of the first.
source_text: In this case, stochastic variations in initial conditions can result in dramatically different patterns, giving rise to a phenomenon equivalent to 'survival of the first'.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference from the model results about antagonistic interactions.

claim: Different patterns have been observed for communities formed by two antagonistic bacteria species.
source_text: Indeed, different patterns have been observed for communities formed by two antagonistic bacteria species (Kuramitsu et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by a citation to Kuramitsu et al., 2007.

claim: The work on ecological patterning is conceptually analogous to the competitive exclusion principle.
source_text: In summary, our work is conceptually analogous to that of the competitive exclusion principle (Gause, 1934).
evidence_reasoning: This is an analogy drawn by the authors to contextualize their work.

claim: The competitive exclusion principle states that two species competing for the exact same resources cannot stably coexist.
source_text: The competitive exclusion principle, also known as Gause's law, states that two species competing for the exact same resources cannot stably coexist.
evidence_reasoning: This is established ecological knowledge supported by a citation to Gause, 1934.

claim: The work on ecological patterning will lay the ground for examining mechanisms that shape patterning in microbial communities.
source_text: our work on ecological patterning will hopefully lay the ground for examining mechanisms that shape patterning in microbial communities.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the work.

claim: Most parameters in the diffusion model were measured experimentally.
source_text: Most parameters in the diffusion model were measured experimentally (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence_reasoning: This describes the empirical basis of the model parameters.

claim: Confocal and two-photon microscopy cannot penetrate deep into yeast communities.
source_text: This is because confocal and two-photon microscopy cannot penetrate deep into yeast communities
evidence_reasoning: This is a known limitation of these microscopy techniques.

claim: Results from the diffusion model underestimated intermixing indexes because a confined cell was modeled to divide strictly vertically upward without allowing cell movements in horizontal directions.
source_text: Results from the diffusion model underestimated intermixing indexes because a confined cell was modeled to divide strictly vertically upward (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) without allowing cell movements in horizontal directions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence_reasoning: This is an explanation for the discrepancy between model and experimental results.

claim: A calculation of the patch size based on experimentally-determined release, diffusion, and consumption of exchanged metabolites yielded results comparable to the observed characteristic patch size.
source_text: Indeed, a calculation of the patch size based on experimentally-determined release, diffusion, and consumption of exchanged metabolites yielded comparable results ('Calculating the characteristic patch size in cooperative yeast communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence_reasoning: This is based on calculations using experimental parameters.

claim: Cooperative benefits are unlikely to be available in large excess because of the potential fitness cost of generating benefits and because of competition for these benefits in the partner population.
source_text: However, cooperative benefits are unlikely to be available in large excess because of the potential fitness cost of generating benefits and because of competition for these benefits in the partner population.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the constraints on benefit availability.

claim: Intermixing was largely insensitive to diffusion kinetics, because the characteristic patch size was related to the diffusion constant by 1/5 power.
source_text: Additional calculations showed that intermixing was largely insensitive to diffusion kinetics, because the characteristic patch size was related to the diffusion constant by 1/5 power ('Calculating the characteristic patch size in cooperative yeast communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence_reasoning: This is based on mathematical calculations of the relationship between patch size and diffusion.

claim: In facultative cooperation, small fitness benefits generated less intermixing than large fitness benefits.
source_text: Using the fitness model, we found that in facultative cooperation, small fitness benefits generated less intermixing than large fitness benefits (Figure 3B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model.

claim: Facultative cooperation should resemble obligatory cooperation if fitness benefits are large for both partners.
source_text: This result is intuitive: facultative cooperation should resemble obligatory cooperation if fitness benefits are large for both partners.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the relationship between facultative and obligatory cooperation.

claim: When only one partner receives a large fitness benefit, facultative cooperation should resemble obligatory commensalism.
